q: According to Dow Theory, markets move in:
e: Dow Theory: three trends — primary (months/years), secondary (weeks), minor (days). Each phase has accumulation, public participation, and distribution sub-phases.

q: RSI value above 70 is generally considered:
e: RSI > 70 = overbought. RSI < 30 = oversold. Note: overbought ≠ automatic sell — strong uptrends often keep RSI > 70 for extended periods.

q: A Hammer candlestick at a support level is typically a:
e: Hammer (small body at top + long lower wick) at a support level signals a bullish reversal — buyers have pushed price back up after sellers tested the low. Confirmation by next candle.

q: A Shooting Star candlestick at a resistance level signals:
e: Shooting Star (small body at bottom + long upper wick) at resistance signals a bearish reversal — buyers tried to push higher but were rejected. Mirror of Hammer at support.

q: After a strong uptrend, a Head and Shoulders pattern signals:
o: Bearish reversal — break of neckline confirms
e: Head and Shoulders (three peaks, middle highest) after an uptrend = bearish reversal pattern. Confirmed when price breaks below the 'neckline' connecting the two troughs. Inverse H&S = bullish reversal.

o: Always RSI as the centre line
e: Bollinger Bands: 20-period SMA as the centre, ±2 standard deviations as the upper/lower bands. Squeeze (bands narrowing) often precedes a big breakout in either direction.

q: MACD generates a bullish signal when:
o: MACD crosses above its signal line
MACD crosses below its signal line
e: MACD (typically 12-26-9): bullish when MACD line crosses above signal line; bearish when crosses below. Histogram = MACD − Signal; zero crossings of histogram = momentum shift.

q: The 50% retracement is a key level in:
e: Standard Fibonacci retracement levels: 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, 78.6% of the prior move. 50% is included by tradition though not strictly Fibonacci. Common bounce/pullback zones.

q: When previously-strong support is broken, that level typically:
o: Becomes new support at a higher level
e: Once a support level is broken, it typically becomes new resistance (and vice versa). Sellers who failed to defend it now sell into any rebound to that level — turning support into resistance.
ADX (Average Directional Index) measures trend strength on a 0-100 scale. ADX > 25 = strong trend; < 20 = weak/no trend. Direction is given by +DI vs -DI lines, not ADX itself.

q: Elliott Wave Theory states that markets move in:
o: 5 impulse waves with the trend and 3 corrective waves against
e: Elliott Wave: 5 impulse waves in the direction of the trend, then 3 corrective waves. Wave 3 is typically the longest and strongest. Fractal — same pattern at all timeframes.

o: A small bear candle followed by a larger bull candle that fully engulfs the bear's body
A doji at a support level
e: Bullish Engulfing: small bear candle followed by a larger bull candle whose body fully engulfs the bear's body. Strong reversal signal at oversold levels.

q: On Balance Volume (OBV) confirms an uptrend when:
o: OBV is rising along with price
OBV is falling while price rises (divergence)
e: OBV rising in tandem with price = healthy uptrend confirmed by volume. Divergence (OBV falling while price rises) is a warning sign — suggests the rally lacks volume support.

q: The Stochastic Oscillator considers a stock overbought when:
e: Stochastic > 80 = overbought; < 20 = oversold. Same idea as RSI but uses different thresholds (80/20 vs 70/30 for RSI).

o: An open price equal (or nearly equal) to the close
e: Doji = open ≈ close, producing a tiny body or none at all. Signals indecision; potential reversal at the end of a strong trend. Confirmation needed from the next candle.

q: Which combination is best for a research analyst's stock-selection process?
o: Use FA to select WHAT to buy and TA to time WHEN
e: Best practice combines both: FA identifies undervalued or growing businesses (the WHAT); TA helps time entries and exits (the WHEN). Single-approach strategies are fragile.

q: A Double Bottom pattern is generally:
e: Double Bottom (W-shape) after a downtrend signals a bullish reversal. Two attempts at a low fail to break it; break above the resistance confirms reversal.

o: The bands narrow significantly, indicating low volatility and a potential big move
e: Bollinger Squeeze: bands narrow significantly = low volatility = often precedes a big breakout in either direction. Direction is not predicted by the squeeze itself; supplementary indicators are used to confirm.
